As she said these words her foot slipped, and in another moment, splash! she was up to her chin in salt water. Her first idea was that she had somehow fallen into the sea, "and in that case I can go back by railway," she said to herself. (Alice had been to the seaside once in her life, and had come to the general conclusion, that wherever you go to on the English coast you find a number of bathing machines in the sea, some children digging in the sand with wooden spades, then a row of lodging houses, and behind them a railway station.) However, she soon made out that she was in the pool of tears which she had wept when she was nine feet high.

What happens to Alice? Tell me in one line.
Alice slips and lands up to her chin in salt water, and soon realises it is the pool of tears she cried when she was very tall.

When, after Karna's fall Partha uttered leonine shouts, a great fright entered the hearts of thy sons. Upon the fall of Karna no warrior of thy army set his heart on rallying the troops or putting forth his prowess. Their refuge having been destroyed by Arjuna, they were then like raftless merchants, whose vessels have wrecked on the fathomless ocean, desirous of crossing the uncrossable main. After the slaughter of the Suta's son, O king, the Kauravas, terrified and mangled with shafts, masterless and desirous of protection, became like a herd of elephants afflicted by lions. Vanquished by Savyasaci on that afternoon, they fled away like bulls with broken horns or snakes with broken fangs. Their foremost of heroes slain, their troops thrown into confusion, themselves mangled with keen arrows, thy sons, after the fall of Karna, O king, fled away in fear.

Summarize this battle scene in one sentence.
After Karna falls and Arjuna roars in triumph, the frightened Kaurava troops lose all courage and flee like a broken herd.

What does Victor see and feel on the climb? Summarize it.

The ascent is precipitous, but the path is cut into continual and short windings, which enable you to surmount the perpendicularity of the mountain. It is a scene terrifically desolate. In a thousand spots the traces of the winter avalanche may be perceived, where trees lie broken and strewed on the ground, some entirely destroyed, others bent, leaning upon the jutting rocks of the mountain or transversely upon other trees. The path, as you ascend higher, is intersected by ravines of snow, down which stones continually roll from above; one of them is particularly dangerous, as the slightest sound, such as even speaking in a loud voice, produces a concussion of air sufficient to draw destruction upon the head of the speaker. The pines are not tall or luxuriant, but they are sombre and add an air of severity to the scene. I looked on the valley beneath; vast mists were rising from the rivers which ran through it and curling in thick wreaths around the opposite mountains, whose summits were hid in the uniform clouds, while rain poured from the dark sky and added to the melancholy impression I received from the objects around me. Alas! Why does man boast of sensibilities superior to those apparent in the brute; it only renders them more necessary beings. If our impulses were confined to hunger, thirst, and desire, we might be nearly free; but now we are moved by every wind that blows and a chance word or scene that that word may convey to us.

Victor climbs a steep, winding mountain path past trees broken by avalanches and gullies where stones fall at the slightest sound. Mist and rain cover the valley below. The gloomy scene makes him reflect that human feelings make people easily moved by every small thing.

Explain this text in three short sentences.

Rashmi, you're leaving for Hyderabad next month, so listen to your Jeevan thatha for once. At nineteen I took the train from Mangalore to Bombay for a mill job. The first week was all noise and wonder. By the sixth week, nobody knew my name. The canteen rice was wrong, the fish was wrong, even the rain smelled wrong. I shared a room with five men from Bihar who were kind, but their jokes went over my head. At night I lay on my mat and cried into my towel so nobody would hear. I wrote to my amma that I wanted to come home. She wrote back, 'Come if you must. But wait till Deepavali first.' I waited. That crying didn't mean I had chosen wrong, kutty. It meant I loved where I came from. Both things were true.

Jeevan thatha tells Rashmi that at nineteen he moved to Bombay for work.
He felt lonely, cried at night and wanted to go home.
He says crying showed he loved home, not that he chose wrong.

Write a summary of this extract under 50 words long.

When the rota changed at the call centre in Gurugram, Dilnaz moved to nights and Tushar stayed on days. For two years they had shared the 1 p.m. canteen table and grumbled about the same customers. Now their only overlap was the ten minutes at shift change, when he was leaving and she was badging in, both too tired to talk. After a month Dilnaz noticed she no longer knew what was going on in his life. So she stuck a note inside his locker: "Samosa + 10 minutes, Friday 9:50 pm, bench by the gate?" On Friday he was there with two samosas and a flask of tea. They didn't solve anything. He told her about his sister's wedding plans; she told him about the man who had sung her a song on a complaint call. It became their Friday. Some weeks it was only five minutes.

When Dilnaz moved to night shifts, she and Tushar lost their daily lunch together. She left a note inviting him to share samosas and tea for ten minutes on Friday. He came, and the Friday meeting became their habit, sometimes only five minutes.

Summarize this in a few short bullet points.

"He investigated the case with great care, for Dr. Roylott's conduct had long been notorious in the county, but he was unable to find any satisfactory cause of death. My evidence showed that the door had been fastened upon the inner side, and the windows were blocked by old-fashioned shutters with broad iron bars, which were secured every night. The walls were carefully sounded, and were shown to be quite solid all round, and the flooring was also thoroughly examined, with the same result. The chimney is wide, but is barred up by four large staples. It is certain, therefore, that my sister was quite alone when she met her end. Besides, there were no marks of any violence upon her."

- The investigator found no clear cause of death.
- The door was locked from inside, and the windows had shutters and iron bars.
- The walls, floor and chimney were checked, and nothing was found.
- The sister had no marks of violence and was alone when she died.

Give me only the main idea.

"But does it not show great weakness?" pursued she. "I'm not envious: I never feel hurt at the brightness of Isabella's yellow hair and the whiteness of her skin, at her dainty elegance, and the fondness all the family exhibit for her. Even you, Nelly, if we have a dispute sometimes, you back Isabella at once; and I yield like a foolish mother: I call her a darling, and flatter her into a good temper. It pleases her brother to see us cordial, and that pleases me. But they are very much alike: they are spoiled children, and fancy the world was made for their accommodation; and though I humour both, I think a smart chastisement might improve them all the same."

A woman says she is not jealous of Isabella, whom the family favours, and gives in to Isabella and her brother to keep the peace. She still thinks they are spoiled and would benefit from a firm scolding.

After a while, finding that nothing more happened, she decided on going into the garden at once; but, alas for poor Alice! when she got to the door, she found she had forgotten the little golden key, and when she went back to the table for it, she found she could not possibly reach it: she could see it quite plainly through the glass, and she tried her best to climb up one of the legs of the table, but it was too slippery; and when she had tired herself out with trying, the poor little thing sat down and cried.

Give me a one-line version of this text.
Alice finds she has left the key on the table, cannot reach it or climb the slippery leg, and sits down and cries.

Put this text into three bullet points.

At length I arrived at the village of Chamounix. Exhaustion succeeded to the extreme fatigue both of body and of mind which I had endured. For a short space of time I remained at the window watching the pallid lightnings that played above Mont Blanc and listening to the rushing of the Arve, which pursued its noisy way beneath. The same lulling sounds acted as a lullaby to my too keen sensations; when I placed my head upon my pillow, sleep crept over me; I felt it as it came and blessed the giver of oblivion.

- The narrator reaches the village of Chamounix, worn out in body and mind.
- From the window, the narrator watches pale lightning over Mont Blanc and listens to the rushing Arve.
- The sound of the river works like a lullaby, and sleep comes as soon as the narrator lies down.

List the key points of this extract as three bullets.

"It is easy for me to be so, for every event of that dreadful time is seared into my memory. The manor-house is, as I have already said, very old, and only one wing is now inhabited. The bedrooms in this wing are on the ground floor, the sitting-rooms being in the central block of the buildings. Of these bedrooms the first is Dr. Roylott's, the second my sister's, and the third my own. There is no communication between them, but they all open out into the same corridor. Do I make myself plain?"

- The old manor-house has only one wing in use, with the bedrooms on the ground floor.
- The sitting-rooms are in the central block.
- Dr. Roylott's room is first, the speaker's sister's second and the speaker's own third, and all open onto one corridor.

I divined, from this account, that utter lack of sympathy had rendered young Heathcliff selfish and disagreeable, if he were not so originally; and my interest in him, consequently, decayed: though still I was moved with a sense of grief at his lot, and a wish that he had been left with us. Mr. Edgar encouraged me to gain information: he thought a great deal about him, I fancy, and would have run some risk to see him; and he told me once to ask the housekeeper whether he ever came into the village? She said he had only been twice, on horseback, accompanying his father; and both times he pretended to be quite knocked up for three or four days afterwards. That housekeeper left, if I recollect rightly, two years after he came; and another, whom I did not know, was her successor; she lives there still.

Summarize this text in under 60 words.

The narrator concludes that young Heathcliff, given no sympathy, became selfish and disagreeable, so the narrator's interest in him faded. Mr. Edgar still wanted news of him, and the housekeeper said he had been to the village only twice, on horseback with his father.

Condense this excerpt into under 65 words.

On the last Sunday of December, in their rented house in Sangamner, Sarika spread her five-year plan on the terrace floor, weighed down with two steel glasses. Her husband, Ujjwal, brought up the tea and sat beside her. 'Every year you do this,' he said. 'Every year the world changes,' she said. She went down the list. 'Finish the B.Ed. Done. Apply for the district school post. Done, got it. Start a tuition batch in the evenings.' She paused. 'Drop this. With the baby coming in May, evenings are gone.' She crossed it out and wrote beside it: 'dropped, baby, Dec.' Then she added one new line. 'The block office is training teachers for the new digital classrooms. I'll apply.' She wrote the reason next to it too. Ujjwal watched her fold the paper back into its plastic sleeve.

Sarika goes through her five-year plan, noting that she has finished the B.Ed and got the district school post. She drops evening tuition because the baby is due in May and adds a new line to apply for digital-classroom training.

"By all means," cried Bingley; "let us hear all the particulars, not forgetting their comparative height and size, for that will have more weight in the argument, Miss Bennet, than you may be aware of. I assure you that if Darcy were not such a great tall fellow, in comparison with myself, I should not pay him half so much deference. I declare I do not know a more awful object than Darcy on particular occasions, and in particular places; at his own house especially, and of a Sunday evening, when he has nothing to do."

Squeeze this into two sentences.

Bingley says they should hear every detail, including height and size, which matter more to the argument than Miss Bennet knows. Bingley jokes that Darcy would get only half as much respect if he were shorter, and is most formidable at home on a Sunday evening.

Explain this paragraph to me in two sentences.

"'"Manu said, 'In this connection is recited the old history of the discourse between Sukra and the high-souled (Daitya) Vali. Once on a time, Sukra of Bhrigu's race approached the presence of Vali, the son of Virochana, while he was ruling the three worlds. The chief of the Asuras, that giver of sacrificial presents in abundance, having worshipped the descendant of Bhrigu with the Arghya (and offering him a seat), sat down after his guest had seated himself. This very topic that thou hast stated relating to the merits attaching to the gift of flowers and incense and lamps, came up on the occasion. Indeed, the chief of the Daityas put this high question to Sukra, that most learned of all ascetics.

Manu retells an old talk between the wise Sukra and Vali, who was then ruling the three worlds. Vali welcomed his guest with respect and a seat, then asked him about the merit of giving flowers, incense and lamps.

At the weekly haat in their village near Hisar, Kiran bought a toy car, a bag of jalebis and a shiny water bottle, all in ten minutes. His father worked in Dubai and sent money home every month. Vikas had four rupees in his pocket and a pang in his chest. He had never had a toy car that wasn't borrowed. Walking home past the mustard fields, he kicked a stone hard. Then Kiran said, 'Can you ask your Dadaji to help me make a kite like yours? Mine from the shop breaks every time.' Vikas thought of Dadaji's hands splitting bamboo and gluing paper, and of their kite that flew higher than anyone's. Families were different. His had something too. 'Come on Sunday,' he said. 'Bring the jalebis.'

Tell me in three sentences what this excerpt says.

At the weekly market, Kiran buys a toy car and treats, while Vikas has only four rupees and feels a pang. Kiran then asks Vikas to have his grandfather help make a kite, because his shop kites keep breaking. Vikas remembers his family has something too and invites Kiran on Sunday, asking him to bring the jalebis.

Give me the short version of this, under 50 words.

Lady Catherine seemed resigned. "Mrs. Collins, you must send a servant with them. You know I always speak my mind, and I cannot bear the idea of two young women travelling post by themselves. It is highly improper. You must contrive to send somebody. I have the greatest dislike in the world to that sort of thing. Young women should always be properly guarded and attended, according to their situation in life. When my niece Georgiana went to Ramsgate last summer, I made a point of her having two men-servants go with her. Miss Darcy, the daughter of Mr. Darcy of Pemberley, and Lady Anne, could not have appeared with propriety in a different manner. I am excessively attentive to all those things. You must send John with the young ladies, Mrs. Collins. I am glad it occurred to me to mention it; for it would really be discreditable to you to let them go alone."
Lady Catherine tells Mrs. Collins that two young women must not travel by post alone, calling it improper, and that John must go with them. She recalls that her niece Georgiana had two men-servants.

Give this excerpt a two-sentence summary.

The school library had a new rule: each Class 4 pair would run the book-return box for a week and enter a quiz at the end. Himani wanted Pallavi as her partner before the teacher had even finished speaking. Pallavi was the tallest girl in class, and she laughed so easily that even the librarian smiled at her. "She'll know all the quiz answers," Himani whispered to her friend. "And she'd never forget anything. She's too nice." On Wednesday, Pallavi left the return box on the bench outside while she went to play. Three books slid out in the rain. In Friday's quiz, Pallavi guessed most answers with a big grin, and they came sixth. Walking out, Himani looked at Pallavi, who was still laughing with everyone. "You're really fun," she said slowly. "But you're not so good at quizzes, na?"

Himani picks Pallavi as her partner for the book-return box and quiz, expecting her to know all the answers. Pallavi leaves the box in the rain, they place sixth, and Himani calls her fun but not good at quizzes.

Henry rejoiced in my gaiety, and sincerely sympathised in my feelings: he exerted himself to amuse me, while he expressed the sensations that filled his soul. The resources of his mind on this occasion were truly astonishing: his conversation was full of imagination; and very often, in imitation of the Persian and Arabic writers, he invented tales of wonderful fancy and passion. At other times he repeated my favourite poems, or drew me out into arguments, which he supported with great ingenuity.

Boil this piece down to one sentence.
Henry shares the narrator's cheer and amuses the narrator with imaginative talk, invented tales, favourite poems and clever arguments.

Describe this bit of text in just three sentences.

Pooja had led the milk collection team in the Anand district cooperative for a year. When she started, drivers and helpers quit every few months. She didn't give speeches. Instead, she learnt every person's name and something about their lives. Bhupen's daughter was writing her Class 10 boards. Kamla's husband had a bad knee. Each morning at the chilling centre, she asked about them. She also told them why the milk mattered: twelve villages, a school's midday meal, the co-op's tiny profits going back to farmers. Last month the private dairy offered Bhupen more money to drive for them. He said no. "Pooja-ben asks about my daughter's exams," he told the others. "Nobody else does." In her second year, not one person on the team left. Their collection times improved too.

Pooja has led a milk collection team in Anand for a year, and drivers and helpers used to quit every few months. She learns each person's name and life, asks about them each morning, and explains why the milk matters. Bhupen turns down a private dairy's offer of more money because Pooja asks about his daughter's exams, and in her second year nobody leaves.

Summarize this piece for a child in three sentences.

Tarun, nine, got his fifty rupees of pocket money on Saturday morning. The village fair was on Sunday, and his sister Ankita had told him about a spinning top with lights that cost forty rupees. But on Saturday afternoon, the sweets man came down the lane with his cart. Tarun bought jalebis, then a coconut barfi, then a packet of colourful toffees. By evening, the money was gone. On Sunday, at the fair, he stood in front of the spinning top, lights flashing. Ankita had kept her money and bought a small drum. Tarun's eyes filled. On Monday he asked Ankita, "How did you not eat the jalebis?" She shrugged. "I kept thinking about the drum."
Tarun gets fifty rupees, and his sister tells him about a spinning top at the fair. But he spends it all on sweets. At the fair, Ankita buys a drum, but Tarun has no money left.
